records.place: Illmitz, in the Seewinkel on the eastern shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Kracher Trockenbeerenauslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein: Trockenbeerenauslese, from shrivelled, botrytised berries of at least 30 degrees KMW
wine.grapes: Welschriesling and Chardonnay most often, with Scheurebe, Traminer and Muskat Ottonel, and Zweigelt in some years; most numbered wines are of one grape, the Grande Cuvée a blend.
wine.sites: Flat vineyards between Illmitz and the shore of the shallow Neusiedlersee, beside the salt pans of the Seewinkel, where autumn mists off the water bring noble rot almost every year.
wine.making: The year's botrytised wines are kept apart, each mostly of one grape. No sugar may be added: the sweetness is the grape's own, left when the fermentation stops. Zwischen den Seen wines are raised in steel tanks or large wooden casks with long contact with their lees, Nouvelle Vague wines in new barriques. Every Trockenbeerenauslese of the year is then numbered, the denser the wine, the higher its number.
wine.glass: Glazed pineapple, candied lemon and mango over honey in the Zwischen den Seen wines, with the toast and vanilla of new oak in the Nouvelle Vague; luscious and dense, yet lifted by fresh acidity, and long.
wine.ageing: Open and fruity on release, it keeps for decades, the fruit slowly giving way to honey, dried apricot and toffee.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, and small pours.

label.means: Prädikatswein from shrivelled, botrytised berries of at least 30 degrees KMW, never sweetened or chaptalised.
The wine's place in that year's collection: the denser the wine, the higher the number, by the house's own account.
Between the lakes: the line raised in steel tanks or large wooden casks, for pure fruit.
New wave, after the French films of the 1950s: the line raised in new barriques.

records.table: Weinlaubenhof Kracher, at Illmitz by the Neusiedlersee, numbers each year's Trockenbeerenauslesen, the denser the wine the higher the number. The Welschriesling from steel or large casks gives glazed pineapple and honey, the Nouvelle Vague wines take new oak, and all are poured small and cold.
records.story: The estate began as a small mixed farm at Illmitz, in the Seewinkel; by the house's own account its farmer had long wanted to make wine, and in 1959 the winery was founded. That same year his son, Alois Kracher (1959 to 2007), was born. Trained as a chemist, the son joined his father's estate at twenty two, in 1981, and turned it towards the botrytised sweet wines that the lake's autumn mists make possible. In the years after the diethylene glycol scandal of 1985, which had wrecked the name of Austria's sweet wines abroad, the Kracher wines went out into the world, and the 1991 vintage won them wide attention. From 1995, as the house tells it, every Trockenbeerenauslese of a year was numbered, the denser the wine the higher its number, each in one of two lines, Zwischen den Seen or Nouvelle Vague. Alois Kracher died of cancer in December 2007, at forty eight, and his son, then in his twenties, took the estate on. A run of Kracher numbers on a list is a lesson in botrytis at one sitting: grape against grape, steel against new oak, and the number telling how dense each wine will be.

others.name: Grande Cuvée Trockenbeerenauslese
others.note: A blended Trockenbeerenauslese, numbered within the year's collection beside the wines of one grape.

others.name: Beerenauslese Cuvée
others.note: Welschriesling and Chardonnay at Beerenauslese ripeness, the lighter way into the house's sweet wines.

others.name: Auslese Cuvée
others.note: Welschriesling and Chardonnay at Auslese ripeness, and lighter again.

traps: The numbers rank density within one vintage, the higher the denser; they are no measure of quality, and the No. 7 of one year is not the No. 7 of another.
Zwischen den Seen and Nouvelle Vague name the vessel and the style, steel or large casks against new barriques, not the sweetness or the site.
Welschriesling is no relation of Riesling, and Ausbruch is Rust's alone, across the lake, never Illmitz's.

cards.front: Kracher Trockenbeerenauslese: what does the number on the label tell you?
cards.back: The wine's place in that year's collection: the denser the wine, the higher its number. It is no measure of quality.

cards.front: Which Kracher line is raised in new barriques, and which in steel tanks or large casks?
cards.back: Nouvelle Vague in new barriques; Zwischen den Seen in steel tanks or large wooden casks.

questions.q: A guest compares two Kracher Trockenbeerenauslesen of one vintage, No. 3 and No. 9. What does the higher number tell the guest?
opts: The wine is denser and sweeter
The wine has spent longer in bottle
The grapes grew on a higher slope
The wine is judged the better of the two
questions.exp: The house numbers each year's Trockenbeerenauslesen by density, the higher the denser and sweeter; the number ranks no quality, and the No. 9 is no older than the No. 3.

questions.q: Alois Kracher joined his father's estate at Illmitz in 1981, at twenty two. What had he trained as?
opts: A chemist
A cooper
A banker
A chef
questions.exp: He trained as a chemist and then turned the family estate to botrytised sweet wine; the estate itself had begun in 1959 as a small mixed farm, not a cooperage.

report: The library record w-kracher-tba and its trap say the numbers identify lots and are no sweetness scale; the house's own definitions page says the denser the wine, the higher its number, as Vinography and a second guide also report, so the record follows the house and the library line should change.

The library has Zwischen den Seen in large neutral cask and the region record's producers line has it in steel; the house says steel tanks or large wooden casks with long lees contact, which the record keeps.
Founded 1959 rests on the house's own history page; the founder, born in 1928 or 1929 by differing accounts and dead in 2010, is described rather than named.

The appellation is given as Burgenland; since the 2020 vintage a Trockenbeerenauslese of the area may also be labelled Neusiedlersee DAC Reserve (Austrian Wine), and whether recent Kracher labels use it was not confirmed.
Left out for want of a second source: the comparative tastings against Château d'Yquem in 1988 and 1993 (one encyclopaedia only) and the renaming of a sweet wine trophy after Alois Kracher in 2008.
Alois Kracher's son, who took over in 2007, is living and is not named; he is already in people.json.

records.place: Rust, on the western shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Ruster Ausbruch
wine.classification: Prädikatswein at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness, at least 30 degrees KMW, from Rust alone
wine.grapes: White grapes of Rust, the blend changing with the bottling: Weissburgunder above all, with Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Welschriesling and Neuburger.
wine.sites: Vineyards within the town limits of Rust, on limestone and schist sloping gently down to the western shore of the lake, whose autumn mists bring noble rot; the Ried Oberer Wald gives one bottling of its own.
wine.making: The shrivelled, botrytised berries are picked by hand, broken out of the bunch, which by the house's account gives Ausbruch its name, and the wine must be pressed, raised and bottled in Rust. No sugar may be added. Recent bottlings ferment and rest in used barriques, the Essenz for close to two years on its fine lees; some older vintages were raised partly in steel.
wine.glass: Candied apricot, orange peel and honey, with the faint toast of a used barrique; sweet and dense, yet lifted by fresh acidity, so that it never turns syrupy, and long and clean on the finish.
wine.ageing: Charming young for its fruit, it lasts for decades, the apricot turning slowly to dried fruit, toffee and honey.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and small pours, beside blue cheese or an apricot tart.

label.means: From the 2020 vintage, Rust's own appellation, reserved for sweet wine from botrytised, naturally shrivelled berries grown in the town.
Wine of a Prädikat, picked ripe and never chaptalised or sweetened: its sweetness is the grape's own.
A bottling of the Pinot grapes, Weissburgunder with Pinot Gris and, in some years, Chardonnay.

records.table: Feiler-Artinger keeps Rust's old sweet wine alive in a baroque house on the town's main street: Ruster Ausbruch, from botrytised berries broken out of the bunch by hand, honeyed and full of candied apricot, yet fresh. Pour it cold, in small glasses.
records.story: Rust, on the western shore of the Neusiedlersee, has lived by sweet wine for five centuries. In June 1524 Mary of Hungary (1505 to 1558) granted its growers the right to burn an R into their casks, and in 1681, as Austrian Wine tells it, the town bought its charter as a royal free town from Emperor Leopold I (1640 to 1705) for sixty thousand gulden and five hundred pails of Ausbruch. In 1936 a couple of the Feiler family bought a baroque burgher's house at Hauptstrasse 3, in the old centre, and made wine there; the husband first bottled it in 1947, and in 1953, by the house's own account, he made Ruster Ausbruch again after the war. The next generation ran the estate with a sister of the family, and from 1985 her married name, Artinger, joined the Feilers' in the estate's name, in the year the glycol scandal shook Austria's sweet wine. In 2016 the law reserved the word Ausbruch to Rust, and from the 2020 vintage Ruster Ausbruch DAC became, in Austrian Wine's words, the country's first origin protected for sweet wine alone, picked at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness. Feiler-Artinger's Ausbruch is the answer to a question every candidate meets: a place, not a technique, and Rust's own.

others.name: Ruster Ausbruch DAC Essenz
others.note: The densest bottling: under ten per cent alcohol and more than three hundred grams of sugar a litre.

others.name: Solitaire
others.note: The red of the house, a blend of Blaufränkisch with the Bordeaux grapes.

traps: Ausbruch is Rust's alone: an Illmitz or Seewinkel sweet wine of the same ripeness is a Trockenbeerenauslese, never an Ausbruch.
Rust lies on the lake's western shore beside the Leithaberg; Illmitz and the Seewinkel lie across the water to the east.
Ausbruch once sat between Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese; from the 2020 vintage Ruster Ausbruch DAC is picked at Trockenbeerenauslese ripeness.

cards.front: Feiler-Artinger's Ruster Ausbruch: where must the grapes grow, and where must the wine be made?
cards.back: Within the town limits of Rust, and it must be pressed, raised and bottled in a Rust cellar.

cards.front: Where does the word Ausbruch come from, as Feiler-Artinger explains it?
cards.back: From the shrivelled berries broken out of the bunch by hand at harvest.

questions.q: A guest asks why Feiler-Artinger may call its sweet wine Ruster Ausbruch when an Illmitz estate may not. Which reason is right?
opts: The name is reserved to the grapes and cellars of Rust
Only Furmint may be used for an Ausbruch
An Ausbruch must age ten years in cask
Only a growers' club may use the word
questions.exp: Since the law of 2016 and the DAC of 2020, Ausbruch is Rust's alone: grapes from the town, pressed, raised and bottled there. No single grape is required, so Furmint is not the reason.

questions.q: In 1681 Rust bought its charter as a royal free town from Emperor Leopold I. What did it pay, as Austrian Wine tells it?
opts: Gold gulden and pails of Ausbruch
A fleet of boats for the lake
Its vineyards on the Leithaberg
A tithe of its grain harvest
questions.exp: The town paid sixty thousand gulden and five hundred pails of Ausbruch. The privilege of branding its casks with an R came earlier, in 1524, from Mary of Hungary.

report: The library lists Furmint among the grapes of the house's Ruster Ausbruch; no source found here names Furmint for Feiler-Artinger, so the record names the grapes the house's vintage pages and Falstaff's entries give (Weissburgunder, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Welschriesling, Neuburger).
Founded is left empty: the house dates its roots to the purchase of the house at Hauptstrasse 3 in 1936 and its founding to the 1930s, and a purchase is not a founding.

The founding couple and the second generation are described, not named, as no dates were found for the dead and the rest are living; the 1947 first bottling rests on two merchants' histories (Cavetta, Walters Feine Weine), the 1953 Ausbruch on the house and both merchants, and 1985 on Falstaff and the Burgenland Vinothek.

The vessels change with the bottling and the vintage: the house's recent sheets give used barriques, Falstaff's entries give barrique, partial barrique with steel, or steel, so the record says recent bottlings and some older vintages.
The 1993 Ruster Ausbruch's trophy at the International Wine Challenge in 1995, told on the house's site, is left out as an award.
Several dates of the second generation's taking over differ between merchants (1955, 1963, 1965) and are left out.

The privilege of 1524 rests on Austrian Wine and on the town of Rust's own anniversary material, whose Latin charter is dated 27 June 1524; the 1681 charter and its price on Austrian Wine and the Burgenländische Heimatblätter.

records.place: Lutzmannsburg in Mittelburgenland, with the cellar at Grosshöflein, Burgenland

wine.name: Blaufränkisch Lutzmannsburg Alte Reben
wine.sites: A selection of old vines at Lutzmannsburg, in the south of Mittelburgenland by the Rabnitz: vines of eighty years and more, some over a century old, in sandy clay over a limestone base, on a plateau the house describes as an ancient volcano.
wine.making: Fermented with its own yeasts, never a cultured one, with a share of whole bunches in some years; the malolactic fermentation and the ageing that follows take place in old oak casks, large and small, for as long as the wine needs, well over a year, so that no new oak shows.
wine.glass: Ripe dark cherry and blackberry with cracked black pepper and violet; rounder and darker than the Neckenmarkt, yet fine boned and savoury, with bright acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after five or so and keeps for two decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Burgundy glass suits its perfume.

label.means: Old vines: here a selection of vines of eighty years and more, some over a century old.
The village in the south of Mittelburgenland where the vines grow.
The broad origin of the federal state, rather than the Mittelburgenland DAC in which the village lies.

records.table: Moric's Blaufränkisch Lutzmannsburg Alte Reben comes from vines of eighty years and more in the south of Mittelburgenland, fermented with native yeasts and rested in old casks rather than new oak. It is dark cherry and black pepper, savoury and fine.
records.story: Moric, said MO-ritz, began with the 2001 vintage. Its maker came from the Velich family of Apetlon, in the Seewinkel, whose estate, Weingut Velich, is a separate house. Through the 1990s much Austrian red wine had chased weight, with long extraction and new barriques, and Moric went the other way. Its founder leased old Blaufränkisch vines, some a century old and closely planted, at Neckenmarkt in the north of Mittelburgenland and at Lutzmannsburg in the south, to compare what each village's soil and air gave the one grape, and took the fruit to a cellar at Grosshöflein on the Leithaberg. There the wines ferment with their own yeasts and rest in old casks for as long as they need, so that the vineyard speaks rather than the oak. In 2005 Mittelburgenland became a DAC for Blaufränkisch alone, yet the Lutzmannsburg is labelled simply Burgenland. Lutzmannsburg, the warmer and flatter of the two villages, on sandy clay over limestone, gives the rounder, darker wine; Neckenmarkt, on a hillside of slate, gneiss and limestone under the Ödenburg hills, the tauter one. Poured side by side, the two Alte Reben are the argument Moric makes: one grape, two villages, two wines.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Neckenmarkt Alte Reben
others.note: Old vines on a hillside of slate, gneiss and limestone under the Ödenburg hills, the tauter, more structured of the pair.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Burgenland
others.note: The entry Blaufränkisch, labelled simply Burgenland, that carries the house's reading of the grape.

traps: Moric is a separate house from Weingut Velich of Apetlon, though the two spring from one family.
Lutzmannsburg lies inside Mittelburgenland, yet Moric's wine is labelled Burgenland, not Mittelburgenland DAC.
Zweigelt is a crossing of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, never another name for Blaufränkisch.

cards.front: Moric Lutzmannsburg Alte Reben: how old are the vines?
cards.back: Eighty years and more, some over a century old, chosen from the village's old parcels.

cards.front: Which two villages give Moric its two old vine Blaufränkisch?

opts: Native yeasts and old casks, no new barriques
A long cold soak in stainless steel
A share of Zweigelt to soften it
A short rest in small new barrels
questions.exp: Moric ferments with its own yeasts and rests the wine in old casks, so no new oak shows; the wine is Blaufränkisch alone, with no Zweigelt.

Rust
Gols

sources.title: Vinography: MORIC, the apogee of Blaufränkisch
Berry Bros and Rudd: 2020 Blaufränkisch, Lutzmannsburg, Alte Reben, Moric

report: The library's trap names the founder's brother and the founder (both living); the record says only that Weingut Velich is a separate estate of the same family, and names neither.
Vine ages differ by source (80 to 100, 85 to 110, over 100); the record says eighty years and more, some over a century old.

The soil at Lutzmannsburg is sandy clay over a limestone base on an old volcanic plateau in the house's own material and a merchant's; the library says heavier clay, which agrees in part. Vinography puts the villages about ten kilometres apart and the house about twenty, so no distance is given.
The library's style line speaks of pale colour; Lutzmannsburg is the darker, rounder of the pair in the library's own wine list and in Vinography, which the glass follows.
The share of whole bunches rests on the library record alone; open wooden vats and about twenty months in old oak rest on one merchant and are left out.
No source found here explains the name Moric, so the story gives only its sound.

records.place: Rust, in the hills above the western shore of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental
wine.sites: The Ried Mariental at Rust: lean, chalky soil, a microclimate of its own and very old vines, as the house describes it; its neighbour, the Oberer Wald, carries more clay and gives a leaner wine.
wine.making: Fermented on its skins, the wine then spends close to two years in small oak barrels of about three hundred litres, most of them new, before it is bottled; it is a dense, oak framed Blaufränkisch, built to be cellared rather than drunk young.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, blackberry and plum over cedar and cocoa, with a stony, chalky edge; firm, fine grained tannin and fresh acidity carry the oak to a long, taut finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and marked by oak when young, it needs about ten years to settle and lasts for twenty and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The named single vineyard at Rust, of lean, chalky soil, that gives the wine its name.
The free town on the lake's western shore, the village named on the label.
The grape, called Kékfrankos in Hungary and Lemberger in Germany.

records.table: Ernst Triebaumer's Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental grows on lean, chalky soil at Rust, and its 1986 vintage opened a new chapter for Austrian red wine. Close to two years in small, mostly new oak make it firm and dark, so give it ten years.
records.story: Rust's growers have made sweet Ausbruch for centuries, and the Triebaumers made it too, but their name travels on a dry red. In 1976, as the house tells it, a Rust couple who felt they lacked the equipment to do justice to their plot in the Mariental sold it to the family. Its lean, chalky soil, its microclimate and its very old Blaufränkisch vines suited a red to keep. The 1986 Blaufränkisch Mariental came a year after the diethylene glycol scandal of 1985 had wrecked the name of Austrian wine abroad, and by the house's own account it had won almost every tasting it entered by 1988; Falstaff dates a new era of Austrian red wine from it. In later vintages the wine has been given close to two years in small barrels of about three hundred litres, most of them new, a firmer frame than the large old casks of much Austrian Blaufränkisch. Beside it the family bottles the neighbouring Oberer Wald, with more clay and rows running north to south, as a leaner, cooler counterpart. When a guest asks where Austria's modern Blaufränkisch began, the Mariental of 1986 is the vintage the story is usually told from.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Ried Oberer Wald
others.note: From the neighbouring site, with more clay and rows running north to south: a leaner, cooler Blaufränkisch.

others.name: Ruster Ausbruch
others.note: The town's sweet wine from botrytised, shrivelled berries, made by the house beside its reds.

traps: Several Triebaumer estates make wine in Rust; the Mariental of 1986 is the Ernst Triebaumer estate's, so read the full name on the label.
Blaufränkisch is Kékfrankos in Hungary and Lemberger in Germany, and Zweigelt is its offspring, never another name for it.
The Mariental is aged in small, mostly new barrels, not in the large old casks of much modern Blaufränkisch.

cards.front: Which vintage of Ernst Triebaumer's Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental marked a turning point for Austrian red wine?
cards.back: 1986, the year after the glycol scandal.

cards.front: Ernst Triebaumer's Ried Mariental at Rust: what soil, as the house describes it?
cards.back: Lean, chalky soil, with a microclimate of its own and very old vines.

questions.q: A guest asks how Ernst Triebaumer's Blaufränkisch Ried Mariental is aged. Which answer is right?
opts: Nearly two years in small new oak
Six months in stainless steel only
Four years in large old casks
A year in concrete eggs
questions.exp: The Mariental rests close to two years in barrels of about three hundred litres, mostly new; large old casks are the way of other Blaufränkisch, not of this one.

questions.q: The Triebaumer family came by its Mariental plot at Rust in 1976. How, by the house's own account?
opts: A Rust couple sold it to the family
It was a gift of the Esterházy princes
The family planted it on cleared forest
It came with a house on the main street

sources.title: Flaschenpost: Blaufränkisch Mariental, Weingut Ernst Triebaumer

report: The library's style line says the Mariental is made without heavy oak; wein.plus and a merchant say it spends close to two years in barrels of about three hundred litres, mostly new, and the record follows them, so the library line should change.
The library calls the Mariental a limestone parcel and its tasting line names slate; the house says lean, chalky soil, which the record keeps, and no source here supports slate.
The library's holdings spell Marienthal; the house and Falstaff spell Mariental, which the record uses.
The appellation is given as Burgenland: dry wines of Rust may carry Leithaberg DAC, and whether recent Mariental labels do was not confirmed.

Left out for want of a second source: the namesake's taking over in 1971 and the longer cask time from 2000 (wein.plus only), a fermentation in steel with wild yeast (one merchant), and the family's presence in Rust since 1691 (one source).

The grower behind the 1986, the house's namesake, is taken to be living (no death was found) and is not named in prose; for people.json, his sons Herbert and Gerhard Triebaumer, who have run the estate since 2001 by wein.plus, are living. The couple who sold the plot are named on the house's page but not here, as no dates were found.

records.place: Schützen am Gebirge, on the Leithaberg west of the Neusiedlersee, Burgenland

wine.name: Blaufränkisch Ried Goldberg
wine.sites: The Goldberg above Schützen am Gebirge, on the slope of the Leitha hills: mica schist under clayey loam, its glittering flecks the gold of the name, as the house tells it. Schist warms quickly, so the Goldberg ripens warmer than the cooler limestone Marienthal.
wine.making: Aged for about two years in wood before bottling. For the 2022 the house's own sheet gives the detail: fermentation in open vats with the cap punched down by hand, about three weeks on the skins, then twenty six months in large casks.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackberry and sloe with cracked pepper and a savoury note of dried herbs over a cool, stony edge; fine grained, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm in youth, it opens after five to eight years and lasts for twenty and more in a warm vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation of the Leitha hills west of the lake; its red is at least 85 per cent Blaufränkisch, from the 2008 vintage.
The named single vineyard above Schützen am Gebirge, on mica schist, recorded since 1555.

records.table: Prieler's Blaufränkisch Ried Goldberg grows on mica schist above Schützen am Gebirge, on the slope of the Leithaberg, and the glitter of the mica is the gold in its name. Aged about two years in wood, it is dark, peppery and firm.
records.story: The Prieler family's roots in Schützen am Gebirge, on the western side of the Neusiedlersee, run deep: the house says the family appears in the village's records as early as 1347, and the Goldberg, the slope of mica schist above the village, is named in documents of 1555. It was the present grower's grandfather, by the house's account, who first put the family's wine into bottles. In 1972 the present grower's parents turned the estate towards quality, towards Blaufränkisch and the Pinot grapes, as two importers' histories tell it. Schist warms easily in the sun, the house explains, so the Goldberg ripens warmer than the family's Marienthal on limestone, and the pair show how one grape answers two rocks. In 2008 the Leithaberg became a DAC for red wine, Blaufränkisch led, and the Goldberg has since come to carry Leithaberg DAC and Ried Goldberg on its label. Beside them the family bottles the Haidsatz, limestone over schist, as a Pinot Blanc of one vineyard. Poured beside a Blaufränkisch from limestone, the Goldberg shows what schist does to the grape: darker, more peppery and firm.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Leithaberg DAC Ried Marienthal
others.note: From the cooler Marienthal on limestone and chalk, the limestone counterpart to the Goldberg.

others.name: Pinot Blanc Leithaberg DAC Ried Haidsatz
others.note: The house's white of one vineyard, Weissburgunder from limestone over schist.

others.name: Blaufränkisch Oggau Johanneshöhe
others.note: From iron rich brown loam at Oggau, aged in large wooden casks.

traps: Prieler's Goldberg at Schützen am Gebirge is a Leithaberg site on mica schist, not the Goldberg of Deutschkreutz in Mittelburgenland.
Schützen am Gebirge lies on the Leithaberg, west of the lake; Deutsch Schützen is a village of the Eisenberg in the far south.
The gold of the Goldberg is the glitter of mica in its schist, by the house's account, not a golden wine.

cards.back: Mica schist; its glittering flecks are the gold of the name, as the house tells it.

opts: Mica schist that warms quickly in the sun
A share of Zweigelt in the blend
Longer ageing in new barriques
Grapes dried on reed mats first

questions.exp: The family is named in the village's records in 1347, by the house's account; the Goldberg itself is named in documents of 1555, in the sixteenth century.

sources.title: Prieler: the family and the estate
Falstaff: Prieler 2016 Blaufränkisch Leithaberg DAC Ried Goldberg

report: The house is not in the library: 1347, the grandfather's first bottling, the Goldberg's record of 1555, its mica schist and the making rest on the house's own pages (1555 also on Smart Wines), and 1972 on two importers (Skurnik, Perrine's).

The vessel differs by source: Falstaff gives barrique for one vintage and the house's own sheet for 2022 gives twenty six months in large casks; the record follows the house and says about two years in wood.
Left out for want of a second source: a single vineyard Goldberg bottled as early as the 1920s (Skurnik only) and a Goldberg made only in the warmest years (one press piece).
Older vintages were labelled Burgenland (wein.plus lists a 2011 as Blaufränkisch Goldberg Burgenland); the appellation given is Leithaberg DAC, which recent vintages carry.
Living and not named, for people.json: the parents of 1972, Engelbert and Irmgard Prieler, and their children, Silvia and Georg Prieler.
The region record's line (Leithaberg DAC Blaufränkisch from the Goldberg's schist, fine and mineral) agrees with the record.
